clinical_knowledge.topic: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management follows an evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP), with drug-induced thrombocytopenia as a key differential, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Sudden petechiae and bruising without trauma
Mucosal bleeding (gum bleeding when brushing teeth)
No new medications to suggest a drug-induced cause
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Drug-induced thrombocytopenia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Mucosal bleeding (gums, nose) — signals higher bleeding risk than skin bruising alone.
management_principles: Check urgent CBC (evaluate platelet count; typical ITP shows isolated thrombocytopenia), peripheral blood smear, and consult hematology
Avoid NSAIDs and other antiplatelet agents
Refer to hematology and provide comprehensive patient counseling
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 48F with sudden onset of petechiae and bruising on her lower legs without trauma, plus gum bleeding with brushing, over the past week.
reference_soap.objective: Multiple petechiae and ecchymoses on bilateral lower extremities. Blood noted at gumline. No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Hemodynamically stable.
reference_soap.assessment: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP); differential includes drug-induced thrombocytopenia.
reference_soap.plan: Check urgent CBC (evaluate platelet count; typical ITP shows isolated thrombocytopenia), peripheral blood smear, and consult hematology. Avoid NSAIDs and antiplatelet agents. Provide comprehensive patient counseling.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP), differential includes drug-induced thrombocytopenia.
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for sudden easy bruising, purple skin spots, and gum bleeding for 1 week
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for hematology & oncology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies for Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP), differential includes drug-induced thrombocytopenia.

teaching.one_liner: Autoantibodies destroy platelets, causing isolated thrombocytopenia that presents as easy bruising, petechiae, and mucosal bleeding (gums) without an underlying cause.
differentials: Leukemia (would show other cell line abnormalities)
TTP (would include hemolysis and neurological symptoms)
red_flags: Mucosal bleeding (gums, nose) — signals higher bleeding risk than skin bruising alone

must_ask.say: How suddenly did the bruising and spots appear?
Did any of these bruises come from an injury, or did they just appear?
Have your gums been bleeding, or any nosebleeds?
Have you started any new medications or products recently?
Do you have any thyroid or autoimmune conditions?
